nodes.name: Ambient temperature
nodes.desc: Ambient temperature refers to the average air temperature in a given environment, measured using a thermometer. nodes.name: Blood pressure

nodes.name: Skin conductance
nodes.desc: Skin Conductance (SC) measures the electrical conductance of the skin, which varies with moisture levels regulated by the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. It is a key indicator of electrodermal activity (EDA) and is closely linked to emotional arousal, stress, and physiological responses. SC is commonly measured using wearable sensors that detect changes in sweat gland activity, providing insights…
nodes.range: Skin conductance typically ranges from 0.01 to 39.95 microsiemens (µS), with higher values indicating increased sympathetic arousal. Units: microsiemens (µS).
nodes.rec: To manage stress and reduce elevated skin conductance levels, practice relaxation techniques such as deep breathing, mindfulness, or meditation. Regular physical activity and maintaining a balanced lifestyle can also help regulate autonomic nervous system activity.

nodes.name: Skin hydration levels
nodes.desc: Skin Hydration Level refers to the amount of water content in the skin, which is a key indicator of skin health and overall hydration status. It is often assessed through the skin's elasticity and ability to return to its original position after being pinched or pressed. Higher hydration levels are associated with supple, soft, and healthy skin, while lower levels may indicate dehydration. Wearable sensors and…
nodes.range: Skin hydration levels typically range between 0-130 arbitrary units (AU), with higher values indicating better hydration. Normal hydration levels vary by body region, with cheeks often showing higher hydration (e.g., 25.0 ± 7.4 AU) compared to drier areas like the back (e.g., 12.5 AU).
nodes.rec: To maintain healthy skin hydration levels: 1) Get 8-9 hours of sleep nightly. 2) Limit showers to 5-10 minutes with lukewarm water. 3) Drink sufficient water daily. 4) Reduce consumption of coffee and alcohol. 5) Avoid or limit smoking. 6) Use gentle cleansers. 7) Consume a diet rich in essential…

nodes.name: Skin temperature
nodes.desc: Skin temperature refers to the temperature of the outermost surface of the body, measured in degrees Celsius (°C) or Fahrenheit (°F). It is influenced by factors such as blood flow, environmental conditions, and metabolic activity. Skin temperature is a key indicator of thermoregulation and can provide insights into physiological states, such as fever, stress, or physical activity. Wearable devices measure skin…
nodes.range: Normal skin temperature on the trunk of the body ranges between 33.5°C and 36.9°C (92.3°F and 98.4°F). Protruding body parts (e.g., nose) may have lower temperatures, while areas over active muscles or organs may have higher temperatures. Units: degrees Celsius (°C) or Fahrenheit (°F).
nodes.rec: To maintain stable skin temperature, engage in regular physical activity to improve circulation, maintain a consistent sleep schedule to support circadian rhythms, and avoid extreme environmental temperatures. Monitor skin temperature using wearable devices to detect abnormalities and adjust…

nodes.name: Sleep breathing rate
nodes.desc: Sleep Breathing Rate (SBR) refers to the average number of breaths taken per minute during sleep. It is a critical metric for monitoring respiratory health and identifying conditions such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Wearable devices estimate SBR using sensors like accelerometers or chest straps to detect chest movements or airflow patterns. A normal SBR indicates efficient respiratory function, while…
nodes.range: Normal SBR varies by age: Children (6-12 years): 18-30 breaths/min, Teens (13-17 years): 13-21 breaths/min, Adults (18+ years): 12-20 breaths/min, Older Adults (60+ years): 12-28 breaths/min. Units: breaths per minute (bpm).
nodes.rec: Maintain a healthy weight, avoid alcohol and sedatives before bed, and practice breathing exercises like the 4-7-8 technique to improve respiratory function. For persistent issues, consult a healthcare provider to evaluate for conditions like OSA.

nodes.name: Sweat rate
nodes.desc: Sweat Rate (SR) refers to the volume of sweat produced by an individual over a specific period, typically measured in liters per hour (L/h). It is a critical metric for assessing hydration needs, especially during physical activity or in hot environments. SR is influenced by factors such as metabolic rate, environmental conditions, and individual physiology. Wearable sensors can estimate SR indirectly by monitoring…
nodes.range: Typical sweat rates range from 0.5 to 2.0 L/h during physical activity, though rates can exceed 3.0 L/h in extreme conditions. Training and heat acclimatization can increase SR by 10-20%. Units: liters per hour (L/h).
nodes.rec: To maintain hydration, aim to replace fluids lost through sweating during exercise. Use sports drinks or electrolyte supplements to balance electrolyte needs. Monitor SR during training to tailor fluid intake strategies, especially in hot or humid conditions.

nodes.name: Temperature Variation
nodes.desc: Temperature Variation refers to the deviation in skin temperature from an individual's long-term average or baseline, typically calculated over a 30-day period. It is a metric used to monitor physiological changes and can indicate variations in health status, such as fever, stress, or environmental exposure. Wearable devices measure this using skin temperature sensors and compare it to the user's historical data to…
nodes.range: Normal diurnal temperature variations in healthy individuals typically range from 0.25°C to 0.5°C (0.45°F to 0.9°F). In extreme environmental conditions, variations can be as high as 40°F to 50°F (22.2°C to 27.8°C). Units: degrees Celsius (°C) or Fahrenheit (°F).
nodes.rec: Monitor temperature variations regularly to identify patterns or anomalies. If significant deviations are observed, consider environmental factors, hydration levels, and potential health conditions. Seek medical advice if persistent or extreme variations occur.

nodes.name: VO2 Max
nodes.desc: VO2 Max, or Maximal Oxygen Consumption, is the maximum rate at which the body can utilize oxygen during intense or maximal exercise. It is a key indicator of cardiovascular fitness and aerobic endurance, often used to assess an individual's fitness level and performance potential in endurance activities like running, cycling, and swimming. Traditionally measured in a lab setting using a treadmill or stationary bike…
nodes.range: VO2 Max values vary by age, sex, and fitness level. For example, average values for adults aged 40-49 are around 26.7 mL/(kg·min) for the 50th percentile, while elite athletes may exceed 90 mL/(kg·min). Units: milliliters of oxygen per kilogram of body weight per minute (mL/(kg·min)).
nodes.rec: To improve VO2 Max, engage in regular aerobic exercises such as running, cycling, or swimming. Incorporate interval training, which alternates between high-intensity bursts and recovery periods, to enhance cardiovascular efficiency. Start with a warm-up and gradually increase intensity to avoid…

nodes.name: Arousals per night
nodes.desc: Arousals per Night (APN) refers to the number of brief awakenings or upticks in brain activity that occur during sleep, typically lasting 3-15 seconds. These arousals are a normal part of the sleep cycle but can increase in frequency with age or due to sleep disorders. Wearable devices estimate APN using sensors like accelerometers or heart rate monitors to detect changes in sleep patterns and physiological…
nodes.range: Normal APN varies by age: 18-20 year olds average 80 arousals per night, 31-40 year olds average 116, and 61-70 year olds average 130. Units: number of arousals per night.
nodes.rec: To reduce excessive arousals, maintain a consistent sleep schedule, avoid caffeine and alcohol before bed, manage stress, and treat underlying sleep disorders like sleep apnea. Creating a calming bedtime routine and optimizing the sleep environment can also help improve sleep continuity.

nodes.name: Asleep duration
nodes.desc: Total Sleep Duration (TSD) refers to the cumulative amount of time spent asleep during a sleep period, measured from sleep onset to wake-up time. It is a key metric for assessing sleep quantity and is critical for understanding sleep quality, health outcomes, and overall well-being. Wearable devices estimate TSD using accelerometers, heart rate monitors, or other sensors to detect sleep stages and transitions.
nodes.range: Recommended sleep durations vary by age: newborns (14-17 hours), infants (12-15 hours), toddlers (11-14 hours), preschoolers (10-13 hours), school-aged children (9-11 hours), teenagers (8-10 hours), adults (7-9 hours), and older adults (7-8 hours). Units: hours.
nodes.rec: Maintain a consistent sleep schedule, create a comfortable sleep environment, avoid caffeine and large meals before bedtime, and engage in regular physical activity. Use wearable devices to monitor sleep patterns and adjust behaviors to meet recommended sleep durations.

nodes.name: Bedtime end time
nodes.desc: Bedtime End Time refers to the specific time at which an individual wakes up and ends their sleep period. It is a critical component of sleep hygiene and circadian rhythm regulation, influencing overall sleep quality and daily functioning. Wearable devices track this metric using accelerometers or heart rate variability to detect wakefulness.
nodes.range: Ideal Bedtime End Times vary by age group: Preschool (3-5 years): 7-8 a.m., School-age (6-13 years): 8-9:30 a.m., Teen (14-17 years): 9-10:30 a.m., Young adult (18-25 years): 8-12 a.m. Units: time (HH:MM).
nodes.rec: Maintain a consistent wake-up time, avoid electronic devices before bed, engage in relaxing activities like stretching or reading, and create a comfortable sleep environment to improve sleep quality and regulate Bedtime End Time.

nodes.name: Bedtime start time
nodes.desc: Bedtime Start Time refers to the specific time an individual begins their sleep period, typically when they get into bed with the intention of sleeping. It is a critical component of sleep hygiene and circadian rhythm regulation, influencing overall sleep quality and duration. Consistent bedtime routines and start times are associated with improved sleep outcomes and better health.
nodes.range: Recommended bedtime start times vary by age group: School-age children (6-13 years): 8:00 - 9:30 p.m., Teens (14-17 years): 9:00 - 10:30 p.m., Young adults (18-25 years): 8:00 - 12:00 p.m., Adults (26-64 years): 8:00 - 12:00 p.m. Consistency is more important than the exact time.
nodes.rec: To improve sleep hygiene, maintain a consistent bedtime and wake-up schedule, create a relaxing pre-sleep routine, optimize the sleep environment (e.g., comfortable bedding, reduced light and noise), avoid stimulating activities or heavy meals before bed, and seek professional help if sleep issues…

nodes.name: Breathing irregularities
nodes.desc: Breathing irregularities refer to deviations from the normal breathing pattern, including changes in rhythm, depth, or rate of breaths. These irregularities can manifest as tachypnea (rapid breathing), bradypnea (slow breathing), or dyspnea (difficulty breathing). They are often indicative of underlying conditions such as heart disease, lung disorders, anxiety, or other systemic issues. Wearable devices can monitor…
nodes.range: Normal respiratory rates are 12-20 breaths per minute for adults, 30-60 breaths per minute for infants, and 12-18 breaths per minute for children. Values outside these ranges may indicate breathing irregularities. Units: breaths per minute (bpm).
nodes.rec: To manage breathing irregularities, practice deep breathing exercises, pursed-lip breathing, and diaphragmatic breathing. Maintain good posture, stay hydrated, and engage in regular physical activity. If symptoms persist, consult a healthcare professional for further evaluation and treatment.

nodes.name: Circadian rhythm patterns
nodes.desc: Circadian Rhythm Patterns refer to the 24-hour cycles of physical, mental, and behavioral changes regulated by the body's internal clock. These rhythms are influenced primarily by light and darkness but are also affected by factors such as food intake, stress, physical activity, social environment, and temperature. They play a critical role in regulating sleep-wake cycles, hormone release, and other physiological…
nodes.range: Circadian rhythms typically follow a 24-hour cycle, though individual variations can range from 23.5 to 24.65 hours. These rhythms are entrained by external cues like light and daily routines.
nodes.rec: To maintain healthy circadian rhythms, establish a consistent sleep schedule, avoid daytime naps, get regular physical activity, and expose yourself to natural light during the day. Limit caffeine and alcohol intake, especially in the evening, and create a bedtime routine to signal your body it's…

nodes.name: Deep sleep duration
nodes.desc: Deep Sleep Duration refers to the total amount of time spent in the deep sleep stage (N3 or slow-wave sleep) during a sleep period. This stage is crucial for physical recovery, immune function, and memory consolidation. Wearable devices estimate deep sleep duration using sensors like accelerometers and heart rate monitors to track sleep stages based on physiological signals.
nodes.range: For adults, deep sleep typically constitutes 13-23% of total sleep time. For example, in an 8-hour sleep period, deep sleep duration should range between 1 to 1.8 hours. Units: minutes or hours.
nodes.rec: To increase deep sleep duration, maintain a consistent sleep schedule, create a relaxing bedtime routine, avoid caffeine and alcohol before bed, and ensure a comfortable sleep environment. Techniques like stress management and warm baths before bed may also promote deeper sleep.

nodes.name: Light sleep duration
nodes.desc: Light Sleep Duration refers to the total amount of time spent in Stage 1 Non-Rapid Eye Movement (NREM) sleep during a sleep period. This stage is characterized by light sleep, where individuals can be easily awakened, and typically lasts for a few minutes, making up about 5% of total sleep time. It is the initial stage of the sleep cycle and serves as a transition between wakefulness and deeper sleep stages.…
nodes.range: Light sleep typically lasts 1 to 5 minutes per cycle, comprising approximately 5% of total sleep time. It can extend to 10-25 minutes in later cycles. Units: minutes.
nodes.rec: To improve light sleep quality, maintain a consistent sleep schedule, avoid electronic devices before bedtime, and engage in calming activities such as reading or taking a warm bath. Limiting daytime naps and creating a sleep-conducive environment can also enhance overall sleep efficiency.

nodes.name: Midpoint of sleep
nodes.desc: The Midpoint of Sleep (MSF) is the clock time that marks the halfway point between sleep onset and wake-up time, excluding periods of wakefulness during the night. It is a reliable marker of an individual's chronotype and is correlated with dim light melatonin onset, reflecting circadian rhythm patterns. Wearable devices calculate MSF using sleep tracking data to assess sleep timing and alignment with circadian…
nodes.range: A healthy MSF typically occurs between 2:00 AM and 4:00 AM, though this can vary based on sociocultural influences and individual sleep patterns. Units: clock time (e.g., 3:15 AM).
nodes.rec: To optimize sleep timing, maintain a consistent sleep schedule, avoid heavy meals before bed, create a restful sleep environment, limit daytime naps, engage in regular physical activity, and manage stress effectively.

nodes.name: Rem sleep duration
nodes.desc: REM Sleep Duration refers to the total amount of time spent in Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep during a sleep period. REM sleep is a critical phase of the sleep cycle characterized by rapid eye movements, vivid dreaming, and heightened brain activity. It plays a vital role in memory consolidation, emotional regulation, and cognitive function. Wearable devices estimate REM sleep duration using sensors like…
nodes.range: REM sleep typically constitutes 20-25% of total sleep time in healthy adults. The first REM cycle lasts about 10 minutes, with subsequent cycles increasing in duration, up to 60 minutes in later stages. Units: minutes.
nodes.rec: To improve REM sleep duration, maintain a consistent sleep schedule, create a relaxing bedtime routine, avoid caffeine and nicotine, exercise regularly, and limit alcohol and heavy meals close to bedtime.

nodes.name: Sleep apnea events
nodes.desc: Sleep Apnea Events (SAE) refer to episodes of paused or shallow breathing during sleep, known as apneas or hypopneas, respectively. These events are a hallmark of sleep apnea, a condition that disrupts restful sleep and can lead to significant health complications, including cardiovascular issues and daytime fatigue. Wearable devices and sensors, such as those measuring oxygen saturation or respiratory effort, can…
nodes.range: Sleep apnea severity is classified using the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI): Normal (<5 events/hour), Mild (5-14 events/hour), Moderate (15-29 events/hour), Severe (≥30 events/hour). Units: events per hour.
nodes.rec: Lifestyle changes such as weight loss, avoiding alcohol and sedatives, and sleeping on your side can reduce sleep apnea events. Medical interventions, including Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) therapy, oral appliances, or surgery, may be necessary for moderate to severe cases. Regular…

nodes.name: Sleep efficiency
nodes.desc: Sleep Efficiency (SE) is the percentage of time spent asleep compared to the total time in bed, calculated as the ratio of Total Sleep Time (TST) to Time in Bed (TIB) multiplied by 100. It is a critical metric in assessing sleep quality and identifying disorders like insomnia, with higher values indicating more efficient sleep. Wearable sensors estimate SE using accelerometers or heart rate variability to determine…
nodes.range: Normal SE is 80%-90% for healthy adults, with values below 80% indicating potential sleep disturbances. Units: percentage (%).
nodes.rec: To improve sleep efficiency, maintain a consistent sleep schedule, avoid screen time before bed, optimize the sleeping environment with reduced light and noise, and engage in relaxing activities before bedtime. Avoid naps, exercise at least 4 hours before bedtime, and limit caffeine and alcohol…

nodes.name: Sleep onset latency
nodes.desc: Sleep Onset Latency (SOL) refers to the time it takes for an individual to transition from full wakefulness to sleep after turning off the lights. It is a key metric in assessing sleep quality and identifying sleep disorders such as insomnia or excessive daytime sleepiness. SOL is typically measured using polysomnography (PSG) or EEG as part of sleep studies. A shorter SOL may indicate sleep deprivation, while a…
nodes.range: Normal SOL for healthy adults is between 10 and 20 minutes. A SOL of less than 8 minutes may indicate excessive sleepiness, while a SOL longer than 20 minutes may suggest difficulty initiating sleep. Units: minutes.
nodes.rec: To improve sleep onset latency, establish a consistent bedtime routine, avoid stimulating activities and screen time before bed, and create a sleep-conducive environment (e.g., dark, quiet, and cool). Moderate exercise a few hours before bedtime can also help reduce SOL. Avoid caffeine and alcohol…

nodes.name: Sleep stages (light, deep, REM)
nodes.desc: Sleep stages are categorized into light sleep (NREM stages 1 and 2), deep sleep (NREM stage 3), and REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep. Light sleep serves as a transition phase, deep sleep is crucial for physical restoration and recovery, and REM sleep is associated with dreaming, memory consolidation, and emotional regulation. Wearable devices use heart rate variability, movement data, and other sensors to estimate…
nodes.range: A healthy sleep cycle typically consists of: NREM stage 1 (5%), NREM stage 2 (45%), NREM stage 3 (25%), and REM sleep (25%). REM sleep duration increases with each sleep cycle, starting at around 10 minutes and extending up to 50 minutes in later cycles.
nodes.rec: To optimize sleep stages, maintain a consistent sleep schedule, create a calming sleep environment, avoid caffeine and heavy meals before bed, and prioritize stress management. Regular exercise and exposure to natural light during the day can also improve sleep quality and duration.

nodes.name: Snoring patterns
nodes.desc: Snoring patterns refer to the acoustic characteristics and temporal sequences of snoring sounds, which can vary based on the underlying cause. Snoring occurs when air flows past relaxed tissues in the throat, causing vibrations. Patterns can be classified as simple (vibration of an open airway) or complex (momentary airway closure, often associated with obstructive sleep apnea). These patterns are clinically…
nodes.range: Snoring intensity can range from mild (40-50 dB) to severe (>60 dB). Complex snoring patterns, characterized by irregular durations (10-100 seconds) and higher frequencies (100-300 Hz), are more indicative of OSA. Units: decibels (dB) for intensity, hertz (Hz) for frequency.
nodes.rec: To reduce snoring, maintain a healthy weight, exercise regularly, and avoid sleeping on your back. Elevate your head during sleep to improve airflow, and consider using nasal strips or mouthpieces. For severe cases, consult a healthcare professional for interventions like continuous positive…

nodes.name: Time after wakeup
nodes.desc: Time After Wakeup refers to the period immediately following waking up, during which individuals transition from sleep to full alertness. This phase is critical for understanding sleep inertia, the grogginess or disorientation experienced upon waking, and its impact on cognitive and physical performance. Wearable devices can track this period using accelerometers and heart rate variability to monitor physiological…
nodes.range: Sleep inertia typically lasts 15 to 60 minutes, though this can vary based on sleep quality, duration, and individual differences. Units: minutes.
nodes.rec: To reduce sleep inertia and improve alertness after waking, expose yourself to natural light, maintain a consistent wake-up time, and engage in light physical activity such as stretching or walking. Avoid prolonged use of electronic devices immediately after waking.

nodes.name: Total sleep duration
nodes.desc: Total Sleep Duration (TST) refers to the cumulative amount of time spent asleep during a sleep episode, measured from sleep onset to sleep offset. It includes all stages of sleep: N1, N2, N3 (deep sleep), and REM sleep. TST is a critical metric for assessing sleep quality and overall health, as insufficient or excessive sleep duration can negatively impact physical and mental well-being. Wearable devices estimate…
nodes.range: Recommended sleep duration varies by age: newborns (14-17 hours), infants (12-15 hours), toddlers (11-14 hours), preschoolers (10-13 hours), school-aged children (9-11 hours), teenagers (8-10 hours), adults (7-9 hours), and older adults (7-8 hours). Units: hours.
nodes.rec: To improve sleep duration and quality, maintain a consistent sleep schedule, create a relaxing bedtime environment, avoid electronic devices before bed, limit caffeine and alcohol intake, and engage in regular physical activity. Aim for the recommended sleep duration based on your age group to…

nodes.name: Wake after sleep onset
nodes.desc: Wake After Sleep Onset (WASO) is a sleep metric that measures the total duration of wakefulness occurring after the initial onset of sleep until the final awakening. It is a key indicator of sleep continuity and quality, with higher WASO values indicating more fragmented sleep. WASO is commonly measured using wearable devices that track sleep stages through accelerometers or heart rate variability.
nodes.range: Normal WASO values vary by age and health status. For healthy adults, WASO is typically less than 30 minutes per night. Values exceeding 30 minutes may indicate sleep disturbances or disorders. Units: minutes.
nodes.rec: To reduce WASO, maintain a consistent sleep schedule, create a sleep-conducive environment (e.g., dark, quiet, and cool), avoid stimulants like caffeine before bedtime, and engage in relaxation techniques such as progressive muscle relaxation or mindfulness meditation. Regular aerobic exercise and…
